t: 2165. Smallest Value of the Rearranged Number
o: Rearrange digits to minimize the value, keeping the sign. For a positive number, sort digits ascending; if the smallest digit is 0, swap the first nonzero digit into the leading position to kill leading zeros (310 -> 103). For a negative number, minimizing the value means maximizing magnitude, so sort digits descending (-7605 -> -7650); negatives never have leading-zero trouble since the leading digit is the largest. |num| <= 1e15 fits in 64-bit integers and doubles.
k: Positive: ascending digit sort, swapping the first nonzero digit to the front if needed.
Negative: descending digit sort maximizes magnitude, which minimizes the value.

a.n: Approach 1: Digit Sort with Leading-Zero Fix
a.i: Sort the digit characters in the appropriate order and repair a leading zero for positives by swapping in the first nonzero digit.
s: Take |num| as a digit string and sort ascending.
If negative, reverse to descending and negate; otherwise swap s[0] with the first nonzero digit.
Convert back to an integer with the original sign.
a.t: O(d log d) for d digits — sorting dominates

a.i: Digits span only 0-9, so a frequency array replaces comparison sorting, giving O(d) time — marginal gain but a nice optimization to mention.
s: Emit digits ascending (positive) or descending (negative), applying the same leading-zero swap for positives.
a.t: O(d) — counting and emitting 10 digit buckets

w: Edge cases: num = 0 (return 0), numbers already containing no zeros, and all-zero interiors like 100 -> 100 for positives (swap brings the 1 forward: 001 -> 100). Pitfall: applying the leading-zero fix to negatives — unnecessary and wrong-headed, since descending order puts the max digit first. Follow-up: rearrange to the maximum instead — flip both rules.
